title: The Heterophily Snowflake Hypothesis: Training and Empowering GNNs for Heterophilic Graphs

problem.claim: Most current GNN architectures assume homophily, which may be inappropriate for heterophilic graphs and can reduce learning effectiveness.

gap.claim: Existing GNN approaches do not adequately support node-specific aggregation hops and patterns in heterophilic graphs.

contributions.claim: A proxy label predictor gives each node a latent prediction distribution that guides whether connected neighbors should be aggregated.
The Heterophily Snowflake Hypothesis characterizes nodes as having unique aggregation hops and patterns.
The proposed approach is intended to guide and facilitate research on heterophilic graphs and beyond.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors state that they are the first to transfer the concept of one node having one receptive field to heterophilic graphs.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report main results on 10 graphs with varying heterophily ratios across 10 backbones.
The authors report scalability experiments across 2, 4, 6, 8, 16, and 32 layers on deep GNN backbones including SGC and JKNet.
The authors report comparisons with the conventional snowflake hypothesis and existing graph pruning algorithms, including efficiency comparisons.

narrative_sequence.summary: GNNs are widely used for graph-based learning tasks.
Homophily assumptions in current GNN architectures may limit effectiveness on heterophilic graphs.
A proxy label predictor produces node-specific latent prediction distributions to guide neighbor aggregation.
The authors introduce the Heterophily Snowflake Hypothesis, under which nodes have distinct aggregation hops and patterns.
The approach is evaluated through graph, backbone, depth, hypothesis, and efficiency comparisons.

source_observation.claim: Nodes in heterophilic graphs may require different aggregation hops and patterns.

interpretation.claim: Uniform receptive fields may be a poor default for heterophilic graph learning.

application.claim: Graph models can consider node-adaptive aggregation decisions based on latent label-prediction information.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish when node-adaptive aggregation is unnecessary or inferior.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the proxy label predictor architecture or training procedure.
The abstract does not report quantitative results or baseline outcomes.
The abstract does not identify the 10 graphs, heterophily ratios, or backbone configurations in detail.
